issues.issue: The preamble contains a stray closing quotation mark and the dangling phrase "as further defined below," which points to no later definition of "Agreement." The defect is cosmetic and would not change any party's rights.

The independent-contractor recital sits against the pervasive COMPANY controls elsewhere (3(ii)(b) policies, 3(ii)(l) inspection, 15(iv)), which a party could argue creates a relationship other than the one declared. The declaration itself is clear, so the tension is one of characterisation rather than contradiction.

COMPANY's right to "eliminate any PRODUCT for any reason" sits against its 3(ii)(e) duty to "deliver the PRODUCTS to DISTRIBUTOR," raising the Lovejoy-type question whether unfettered elimination could nullify the supply obligation. Section 5(i) partly reconciles them by preserving accepted orders.

"AUTHORIZED CHANNEL OF TRADE" is defined as "retail grocery store outlet customers only," a boundary that is not obviously applied to hybrid or mass-merchandiser food retailers. The definition also fuses the customer class and the territory in one sentence, leaving "CUSTOMERS" ambiguous as to whether it means all grocery outlets or only those actually served.

The grocery-only definition cannot be squared with 3(ii)(a)(1), which permits sales to Kmart and to "specific customers as approved by COMPANY," and with Exhibit B's express statement that DISTRIBUTOR may distribute to Kmart. Kmart is a mass merchandiser, not a retail grocery outlet.

"Good Industry Practice" is keyed to standards "universally accepted and followed in the baking industry," a benchmark that is both vague and, as "universally," impossible to satisfy literally. The open-ended "including, but not limited to" list leaves the catch-all's reach undefined even though breach of the standard triggers termination under 12(iii)(b).

The term clause says the Agreement "shall continue until December 31, 2010, and shall continue in effect until either party terminates" on ninety days' notice, which can be read either as a fixed two-year term or as an evergreen agreement terminable at will. The two readings produce opposite results on whether termination after 2010 requires any reason at all.

Section 2 lets either party terminate on ninety days' notice with no reason stated, while Section 12(i) permits ninety-day termination only "for good cause" or on a change in COMPANY's business; the two cannot both be the exclusive route out. Section 2's opening "Subject to Section 12" does not resolve which prevails.

COMPANY's power to "determine the TERRITORY and AUTHORIZED CHANNEL OF TRADE" unilaterally is hard to reconcile with Section 1(iii) and Exhibit A, which fix the TERRITORY by a signed schedule, and with Section 15(iii)'s requirement that amendments be by written instrument executed by both parties. Read literally it would let COMPANY erase the distributor's territory entirely, the Lovejoy problem.

The service obligations "will consist of, but are not limited to" four enumerated items, leaving the open-ended residue of required in-store service undefined; and "guaranteed sales" is defined only as credit "for all stale and damaged products." The paragraph numbering also runs (1) then (ii), obscuring whether the service duty is a separate obligation or a subpart of the sales restriction.

The permission to sell to Kmart and to "specific customers as approved by COMPANY" conflicts with Section 1(iii), which limits the AUTHORIZED CHANNEL OF TRADE to "retail grocery store outlet customers only," and with 3(ii)(c)'s bar on any other channel of trade. Which text controls a Kmart or approved non-grocery sale is unresolved.

After two specific prohibitions the clause adds that DISTRIBUTOR "must meet certain other guidelines that the COMPANY may determine in its discretion from time to time," an unbounded catch-all appended to an enumerated list. Neither "Wholesaler operations" nor "bid process" is defined.

The ban on wholesaler operations without in-store service is in tension with 15(ii)(a), which expressly permits DISTRIBUTOR to conduct business through subdistributors. Whether servicing stores through an independent distributor is prohibited "Wholesaler operations" is left open.

The obligation to adhere to standards "as shall from time to time be promulgated, altered, amended or modified by COMPANY" has no limit and no defined content, so the scope of the promise cannot be fixed from the text. The sentence is also broken by stray subsection markers, obscuring where the obligation ends.

A duty to follow policies COMPANY may unilaterally change conflicts with Section 15(iii), which permits modification of the Agreement "only by a written instrument duly executed by the parties." A court would have to decide whether a policy change is an amendment.

The bar on selling to "retail stores serviced by the Kellogg's Snacks DSD division" identifies the excluded stores by a shifting factual condition the DISTRIBUTOR cannot verify, and the clause fixes no time at which service is measured. The prohibition's boundary therefore moves.

The disclaimer that DISTRIBUTOR has no exclusive rights to "any stores or designated geography" sits against Exhibit A's grant of a defined TERRITORY and Exhibit B's grandfather of existing customers. Whether any protected book of business survives is unclear.

The prohibition on selling "in any AUTHORIZED CHANNEL OF TRADE other than as stated herein" is a drafting error: the authorized channel is by definition the permitted one, so the sentence forbids what it elsewhere allows and should read "any channel of trade other than" the authorized one. The 30-day effectiveness clause is also mangled ("effective thirty days of receipt").

COMPANY's right to revise Exhibit B "without notice in the sole discretion of COMPANY" conflicts with Section 15(iii), which allows modification of the Agreement and its exhibits only by a written instrument executed by both parties, and with Exhibit B's own grandfather clause for existing customers. Which text governs a unilateral channel change is left open.

The clause conditions COMPANY's duty to use "commercially reasonable efforts" on "sales which are in conflict with Paragraph 3(a)(i) above," but there is no Paragraph 3(a)(i) in this Agreement. The cross-reference error leaves the trigger for the obligation unidentifiable.

The promise to resolve channel conflicts is hard to reconcile with 3(i) and 3(ii)(k), which reserve to COMPANY an absolute right to appoint other distributors and sell in the TERRITORY without liability. The efforts obligation may be read as illusory.

Making COMPANY's own decision "final and binding" on disputes about customer, channel and geographic status is a wholly one-sided allocation of the interpretive question, and "status" is itself undefined. A genuine ambiguity in its reach would be construed against COMPANY as drafter.

A COMPANY-decides-everything clause is difficult to square with 3(ii)(d)'s promise of commercially reasonable efforts to resolve channel conflicts and with the mutual termination and cure machinery of Section 12. Whether it ousts judicial review of channel disputes is unresolved.

The flat duty that COMPANY "shall deliver the PRODUCTS" is contradicted by 3(ii)(g), which lets COMPANY cancel any delivery in whole or in part, cut quantities and discontinue items in its sole discretion without liability. Read together the supply obligation may be entirely illusory.
"Any cause beyond its control" is undefined and has no illustrative list, so the events excusing performance cannot be bounded from the text. The excuse is also available only to COMPANY.

The unlimited right to cancel deliveries, cut quantities and discontinue items "without incurring any liability" cannot be reconciled with 3(ii)(e)'s obligation that COMPANY "shall deliver the PRODUCTS," nor with Section 5(i), which preserves the parties' obligations under accepted orders after a product is eliminated. One provision creates a duty the other cancels.

COMPANY's record-keeping duty has no corresponding audit or access right for DISTRIBUTOR, whereas Section 14 gives COMPANY full audit rights over DISTRIBUTOR's books. The asymmetry is a gap rather than a contradiction.
COMPANY's right to call on customers in the TERRITORY overlaps with 3(i) and 3(ii)(k) but adds no limit on converting those calls into direct sales. The provisions are consistent as drafted.

The reserved right to sell in the TERRITORY "to customers other than the CUSTOMERS" turns on the defined/undefined customer distinction in Section 1(iii), and read broadly it could nullify the distributorship in the Lovejoy sense. Section 3(ii)(d)'s conflict-resolution promise pulls the other way.

The clause grants inspection "[w]ithout notice ... at any time during normal business hours" while also promising "reasonable efforts not to disturb the operations," an unmeasured qualifier on an otherwise unqualified right. The tension is mild and internal.

The subsection bans "competitive cookie, cracker, and wholesome snack products" yet in the next sentence expressly authorises TastyKake and Stella D'oro "cake, cookie, cracker and snack products," so the same goods appear both prohibited and permitted. It also mislabels itself as "subsection 'I'" and states that consent shall "not unreasonably withheld," leaving the consent standard grammatically broken.

The catch-all bar on "any activities whatsoever ... involving any other products which may reasonably be deemed as injurious" sits against the specific Nabisco/Pepperidge Farm list and the notice-and-consent procedure, leaving unclear whether unlisted products are competitive only if COMPANY reasonably says so. Section 12(iii)(b) then makes that judgment a termination trigger in COMPANY's "sole discretion."

"DISTRIBUTOR and COMPANY agree to share in the cost" of required data-processing equipment fixes no proportion, and the reimbursement promise is only "on such terms and in such amounts as COMPANY reimburses its other DSDD distributors," an unascertainable measure. Both obligations lack any figure a court could enforce without extrinsic evidence.

The reimbursement promise is conditioned on COMPANY making the equipment mandatory "on or before July 10, 2010," a date falling within a term that Section 2 says ends December 31, 2010, so the interaction with any successor agreement is unaddressed. The condition is otherwise self-contained.

"Short dated" is defined only as "products whose expiration dates are approaching in the near future," a circular definition with no measurable boundary. "Stale (as indicated expiration date)" is likewise garbled.

Standards "as are conducive to maintenance and furtherance of the reputation and sale of the PRODUCTS" supply no ascertainable content, yet failure to meet them is a termination trigger under 12(iii)(b). The obligation's boundary cannot be applied from the words.
"[I]nformation as to the credit standing of itself" leaves the referent of "itself" grammatically uncertain as between DISTRIBUTOR and COMPANY. The likely meaning is recoverable from context.

The bar on any employee, agent or independent contractor of DISTRIBUTOR being a third-party beneficiary sits alongside 15(ii)(a), which requires subdistributors to sign Exhibit C directly with COMPANY, creating a direct undertaking to COMPANY. The two are reconcilable but their boundary is untested.

The exception for "accounts where COMPANY is responsible for accounts receivable (e.g. Kmart)" identifies the excepted class only by a single example, leaving the reach of the carve-out to ejusdem generis argument. Which further accounts qualify cannot be read off the text.

Making DISTRIBUTOR "solely responsible for any and all promotions, sales and marketing programs, advertising" conflicts with 10(ii), which forbids DISTRIBUTOR from using any advertising or descriptive literature pertaining to PRODUCTS without COMPANY's prior written consent. Sole responsibility and prior-consent control cannot both operate unqualified.

The settlement recital says "Said sum of arrived at as follows," and its arithmetic rests on an "approximate $30,000.00" credit that must in fact be exact for the stated $5,250.71 to follow. The mismatch between an approximate input and an exact output invites a dispute over what credits were actually settled.

The clause settles claims arising from a November 14, 2006 writing, while 15(vii) provides that this Agreement "wholly cancels, voids, and supersedes any agreement heretofore entered into." Whether the pre-existing credits survive the merger clause is a live question.

"[S]uch terms as established by COMPANY from time to time" leaves the price and payment terms entirely at one party's election, with no stated benchmark other than 30 days' notice. Whether "terms" includes the fixed payment terms in 4(v) is not stated.

COMPANY's freedom to change "the terms" on 30 days' notice sits against 4(v), which fixes net-30 payment terms and a 1% fifteen-day discount, and against 15(iii)'s written-amendment requirement. Which prevails on a unilateral change of payment terms is unresolved.

The minimum is stated for products shipped from a DSD Grocery Distribution Center "and" a Non Grocery Distribution Center, where "or" is plainly meant; read literally the 50-case minimum applies to no shipment. The error is small but changes the sentence's operation.

The clause allows price revision "upon thirty (30) days written notice" and in the same sentence "the right at any time to issue new price lists and to change the prices," so the notice condition either governs or is dispensed with. The sentence also breaks off mid-phrase at "and other provisions."

Title passing "absolutely" on delivery is qualified by 12(vi), under which DISTRIBUTOR grants COMPANY a security interest in all PRODUCTS in its possession, and by 12(iv)'s repurchase and repossession rights. These are reconcilable as a sale plus a security interest, but the word "absolutely" invites argument.

The requirement that DISTRIBUTOR pass through 100% of an allowance it funds 25% of interacts with the Operating and Cash Discount definitions and with 4(v)'s payment terms, but no ordering conflict appears. The worked example resolves the calculation.

The cash discount is keyed to a "designated number of days the COMPANY has allowed in its current credit terms," leaving the discount period unfixed on the face of the Agreement. The percentage of the discount is not stated at all.

This open-ended cash discount conflicts with 4(v), which fixes a specific 1% discount for payment within fifteen (or twenty) days; the two describe the same benefit on different terms. Which controls a payment made early is unresolved.

Payment runs "thirty (30) days from the date of receipt for all orders received," which is ambiguous as between receipt of the goods and receipt of the invoice. The discount clause repeats the same undefined "date of receipt."

The fixed net-30 terms and 1% discount conflict with Section 4's opening sentence, under which terms are "established by COMPANY from time to time" and changeable on 30 days' notice, and with the Cash Discount definition's reference to COMPANY's "current credit terms." One of the three must yield.

Preserving obligations under accepted orders after a product is eliminated sits against 3(ii)(g), which lets COMPANY cancel any delivery in whole or part and discontinue any item "without incurring any liability." Whether an accepted order survives a discretionary cancellation is a genuine question.

The statement that the Agreement "may be modified only in accordance with the procedures set forth herein" points to 15(iii)'s mutual-written-instrument rule, yet several clauses (3(ii)(b), 3(ii)(d), Section 4) let COMPANY alter terms unilaterally. The internal reference does not identify which procedure governs.

The commitment to deliver within five business days of the scheduled date is difficult to reconcile with 3(ii)(g), under which COMPANY "assumes no liability ... for delays in delivery." A late delivery would engage both provisions at once.

Making replacement or credit the "sole remedy" for breach of the Paragraph 8 guarantee is in tension with Section 13(i)'s mutual indemnity for losses caused by breach of the Agreement and with 12(v)'s damages cap. Whether the sole-remedy limit survives an indemnity claim is unresolved.

Claims must be reported "as soon as possible, but no later than 24 hours after becoming aware," a period that runs from an unfixed subjective moment of awareness. The consequence of late reporting is not stated in this clause.

The 24-hour bar is hard to square with 7(iii), which contemplates claims for products delivered with less than sixty days of remaining shelf life, a defect that may only become apparent later. Whether the deadline forfeits such claims is not addressed.

The phrase "some other evidence of deficiency which COMPANY shall specify, including but not limited to products received with less than sixty (60) days of remaining shelf life" is garbled: the sixty-day item is a category of defective product, not a form of evidence. It is unclear whether short shelf life is itself a ground for credit or merely proof of one.

Credit is made to depend on "policies and standards set and established from time to time by COMPANY," which conflicts with 15(iii)'s requirement that the Agreement be modified only by mutual written instrument and with 7(i)'s stated rejection right. The unilateral policy power can defeat the express remedy.

The proviso excluding "PRODUCTS ... manufactured by DISTRIBUTOR and shipped under DISTRIBUTOR'S labels" cannot be squared with Section 1(ii), which defines PRODUCTS as goods authorized by COMPANY for sale to DISTRIBUTOR, or with 3(ii)(e) under which COMPANY supplies them. The carve-out appears to describe a transaction this Agreement does not contain.

"COMPANY shall supply" is immediately qualified by "at COMPANY'S sole discretion" and "as may be available to COMPANY," so the sentence states both a duty and an unfettered discretion not to perform it. The catch-all in (d), "such other promotional information and assistance as may be available," compounds the indefiniteness.

The bar on using "any packing materials, descriptive literature, advertising, etc." without prior written consent conflicts with 3(ii)(v), which makes DISTRIBUTOR "solely responsible for any and all promotions, sales and marketing programs, advertising." One clause gives control, the other assigns sole responsibility.

"[T]he General market information regarding the TERRITORY" is undefined and capitalised inconsistently, giving no boundary to what must be handed over on request. The obligation is short but its content is unascertainable.

The confidentiality duty covers "any and all business and technical information pertaining to the COMPANY and/or the PRODUCTS" with no carve-out for publicly available or independently obtained information and no time limit. The open-ended "includes but is not limited to" leaves the protected category unbounded.

"[G]ood cause" is defined as breach "not cured within those times specified below," yet the clause simultaneously requires ninety days' written notice, so it is unclear whether the ninety days runs before or after the cure period. "[A] change in COMPANY's business that results in COMPANY no longer using Independent DSDD distributors in this territory" is a further undefined trigger resting entirely on COMPANY's own conduct.

Requiring good cause and ninety days' notice cannot be reconciled with Section 2, which lets either party terminate on ninety days' notice without any cause, nor with 12(ii) and 12(iii), which permit immediate termination or termination after a five-business-day cure period. The three termination regimes give inconsistent answers to the same facts.

"Make a material change in the control of DISTRIBUTOR'S company that is unacceptable to COMPANY" makes the trigger turn on COMPANY's unexpressed subjective judgment, and neither "material change in control" nor "unacceptable" is defined. Item (f)'s "threatens to do substantial harm to the COMPANY'S business or commercial reputation" is equally open.

Immediate termination for an attempted assignment sits against 15(ii)(a), which declares any such attempted assignment simply "void and without effect," and against 12(i)'s definition of good cause as an uncured breach requiring ninety days' notice. The remedies for the same act differ across the instrument.

The clause gives "five (5) business days written notice" and then measures the cure by "said five (5) day period," so it is unclear whether the cure window is five business days or five calendar days. The difference determines whether a termination was premature.

A five-day cure followed by termination cannot be squared with 12(i), which requires ninety days' written notice for termination for good cause defined by reference to these very cure periods. Section 2's ninety-day notice compounds the mismatch.

The parenthetical exempting "isolated, but not systemic" failures to remove out-of-date merchandise unless they occur more than six times is inserted in the middle of the two-strikes proviso, so it is unclear which rule governs a repeated service failure. "[I]solated, but not systemic" is itself an unmeasured distinction.

Termination for failures that are material "in the sole discretion of COMPANY" after a five-day cure conflicts with 12(i)'s requirement of ninety days' notice for good cause and with Section 2's notice period. It also cross-refers to "(i), (ii), or (iti)(a)" using a mis-typed numeral.

The sentence closes with a stray "for.)." and its repurchase price, "DISTRIBUTOR'S net warehouse cost," is not defined anywhere in the Agreement. What deductions or freight are included in that cost is left open.

The obligation to hand back "free of charge" all products COMPANY previously supplied at no charge sits against 4(iii), under which all PRODUCTS are sold to DISTRIBUTOR "absolutely" with title passing on delivery. Which goods fall on each side of that line is unclear.

The clause says neither party "shall be liable ... for any consequential, punitive or incidental damages ... in any cumulative amount greater than" 50% of a year's gross sales, which reads either as an outright exclusion or as a cap permitting such damages up to that figure. The two readings are irreconcilable and decide whether lost profits are recoverable at all.

If read as a cap it conflicts with Section 13(i)'s unqualified indemnity for "any and all claims, demands, costs, expenses ... and liabilities or losses" caused by breach, and with 7(i)'s sole-remedy provision. The instrument gives no ordering rule between them.

The self-help repossession right "without the need for any further consent or notice" sits against 12(iv)'s repurchase machinery and 4(iii)'s absolute passing of title, and gives no standard for when indebtedness is due. The clauses are reconcilable but their interaction on termination is untested.

The two-year period runs from when "the harm that gave rise to the cause of action arose," a trigger different from accrual and undefined for continuing or later-discovered harm. When the clock starts is exactly the sort of question this wording invites.

The limitation period interacts with 12(v), which measures damages by gross sales "in the twelve months immediately preceding the date upon which an action or proceeding is commenced," but the two use different reference dates. No provision reconciles them.

An indemnity covering losses caused "by a breach of this Agreement by ... the indemnifying party" makes each party indemnify the other for first-party breach damages, which cannot easily be squared with the 12(v) limitation on liability or 7(i)'s sole-remedy clause. Whether the indemnity overrides the damages cap is unresolved.
The mutual insurance obligation is asymmetric in its excess-coverage and certificate requirements, but nothing in the instrument contradicts it. The dollar amounts are specific and self-executing.

The audit right is exercisable "at reasonable times and in its sole discretion" while access is "limited to services performed for COMPANY," yet the record-keeping duty covers "all of its operations and transactions relating to this Agreement." The scope of records that must actually be produced is therefore uncertain.

The effective-date sentence provides only for receipt "by mail, if sent only by mail service, or facsimile," leaving personal service and overnight courier — both authorised methods in the same clause — with no stated effective date. That gap matters directly to the ninety-day and five-day notice periods elsewhere.

Because the notice machinery does not fix an effective date for courier or personal delivery, its interaction with the strict notice periods in Section 2 and Section 12 is left open. Whether a validly served notice started the clock could turn on this omission.

The clause slips into first person — "an assignment effected with our prior written consent" — in an agreement that otherwise refers to COMPANY and DISTRIBUTOR, leaving the consenting party identified only by inference. It also declares attempted assignments both "void and without effect" and "a material breach," which are inconsistent characterisations.

Treating any attempted assignment as void conflicts with 12(ii)(a), which treats the same act as a ground for immediate termination with consent "not to be unreasonably withheld," and with 15(ii)(a)'s express permission to use subdistributors. The instrument gives three different consequences for transfers of the distributorship.

The consent standard is self-cancelling: COMPANY "will not unreasonably withhold" consent but it "will not be unreasonable" to impose the listed conditions "among other requirements," an open-ended catch-all that can swallow the reasonableness promise. The clause also lapses into "we" and "us" without defining those pronouns.

Condition 5, under which execution of a new DSDD Agreement "will terminate this Agreement," adds a termination route absent from Section 12's otherwise comprehensive termination provision and from Section 2's successor-agreement mechanism. Whether an assignment can terminate the Agreement outside Section 12 is unresolved.

Permission to conduct business through subdistributors conflicts with 15(ii)(a), which treats DISTRIBUTOR's services as personal and voids any transfer of the Agreement "in whole or in part," and with 3(ii)(a)(iii)(A), which forbids wholesaler operations where in-store service is not given to individual outlets. Whether using independent distributors is permitted or a material breach is genuinely open.

COMPANY's free right to assign is the mirror opposite of the elaborate restrictions imposed on DISTRIBUTOR in the same subsection, but the asymmetry is expressly stated rather than contradictory. Nothing elsewhere qualifies it.

The requirement that modification be "only by a written instrument duly executed by the parties" cannot be reconciled with 3(ii)(d), which lets COMPANY revise Exhibit B "from time to time without notice in the sole discretion of COMPANY," nor with 3(ii)(b) and Section 4's unilateral changes to policies, prices and terms. Exhibits are expressly part of the Agreement under 15(vii).
The non-agency provision duplicates Section 1(i) and adds a further indemnity, overlapping with 3(ii)(v) and 13(i) without any priority rule. The overlap is cumulative rather than contradictory.
Delaware law is chosen although neither party is located there and performance is in New York and neighbouring states, which could raise a choice-of-law challenge. The clause itself is unambiguous.

The merger clause is qualified by "except as otherwise expressly provided herein" without identifying any such exception, leaving the reach of the supersession open. Its scope is limited to "the subject matter thereof," itself undefined.

The clause supersedes all prior agreements between the parties, yet 3(ii) settles claims arising under a November 14, 2006 writing and preserves accrued credits owed by COMPANY. Whether those pre-existing obligations survive the merger clause is a genuine question.
"[E]ach of which shall be deemed the original" should read "an original"; taken literally it makes every counterpart the single original. The error has no practical consequence.

The TERRITORY — the central grant of the Agreement — is handwritten and substantially illegible ("Py, N'T) PA, Cann."), so the states covered cannot be determined from the document. Whether the territory extends to whole states or parts of them is likewise unstated.

Exhibit A purports to fix the TERRITORY, but 3(i) gives COMPANY the right to "determine the TERRITORY" unilaterally during the term and 3(ii)(c) says DISTRIBUTOR has no exclusive rights to any designated geography. The exhibit's grant and the operative text pull in opposite directions.

The excluded channels are given almost entirely by "e.g." examples and undefined trade categories such as "Specialty stores," "Chain Warehouse programs" and "Mid tier stores," leaving the boundary of each class to argument. Whether a given retailer falls inside an exclusion cannot be read off the list.

The carve-out permitting distribution to Kmart contradicts the exclusion of "Mass merchandisers" in the same line and cannot be squared with Section 1(iii), which limits sales to "retail grocery store outlet customers only." Kmart is both permitted and outside the authorized channel of trade.

The grandfather runs "until further notice from COMPANY" and covers "any of its customers as of the date hereof," neither of which fixes a determinable set of accounts or an end date. Whether an account existed "as of the date hereof" and what notice suffices are both left open.

Permitting continued sales into excluded channels contradicts 3(ii)(d), which flatly prohibits selling to the customers and channels on Exhibit B and makes any such sale a breach subject to termination, and Section 1(iii)'s grocery-only limitation. The exception and the prohibition cover the same conduct.

Exhibit C is titled "DSDD INDEMNIFICATION" and is required by 15(ii)(a) under that name, yet it contains no indemnity obligation at all, only acknowledgments and disclaimers. What a subdistributor is actually undertaking is therefore uncertain.

The prohibition turns on effects "as determined by Kellogg in its sole and absolute discretion," making the standard of breach entirely subjective and unreviewable on its face. The open-ended "nor fail to take any actions" has no boundary.

Kellogg's direct-sales right is limited "to the extent permitted by the agreement then in effect between Kellogg and Premier," yet 3(i) and 3(ii)(k) of that agreement give Kellogg unrestricted rights to sell in the territory. The cross-reference makes the limitation empty.
The sentence reads "the composition of the goods constitution Products," a garbled phrase that obscures what Kellogg may change. The meaning is recoverable but the words as written do not state it.

The disclaimer reads "a third party beneficiary or any agreement," where "of" is plainly intended; as written the sentence does not say what the subdistributor is disclaiming. The error is obvious on its face.

The restriction operates only where the expansion has an effect "as determined by Kellogg in its sole and absolute discretion," so whether conduct breaches the clause depends entirely on one party's unexpressed judgment. No objective standard is supplied.

The clause reads "between the terms and conditions set forth herein as those set forth in any such agreement," where "and" is plainly meant, leaving the comparison ungrammatical. The intended sense is nevertheless clear.

Exhibit C makes its own terms override any Premier–subdistributor agreement, but 15(vii) of the main Agreement provides that this Agreement with its exhibits is the entire agreement between COMPANY and DISTRIBUTOR, and 15(ii)(a) permits subdistribution generally. Which instrument governs a conflict touching all three parties is not addressed.
